notes.meaning: Some time later, two high officials of Pharaoh's court got into trouble with the king. The cupbearer served the king's drinks, and the baker was in charge of his food. Both were men of great rank who stood close to the king. We are not told what they did, though some old writers guessed they were accused of trying to poison him.

Pharaoh's anger put these men in the very prison where Joseph was held. The prison was part of the house of the captain of the guard, Potiphar. Matthew Henry notes that high places are slippery, and that God was quietly using all this to help Joseph. The Geneva Notes say God works in many wonderful ways to rescue his people.

The captain of the guard put Joseph in charge of these two men. Keil & Delitzsch say this meant waiting on them, not guarding them, out of respect for their high rank. Several writers think Potiphar was beginning to see that Joseph was innocent. The men stayed in prison for a while, and we are not told how long.

On the same night, both men had a dream. Each dream fitted what was going to happen to the man who dreamed it. So these were not ordinary dreams but messages about the future. The writers see God's hand here, because he can reach people's minds whenever he chooses.

Joseph noticed their sad faces and asked what was wrong. Matthew Henry says it was the dreams, more than the prison, that troubled them. Joseph's own suffering had made him gentle toward others in trouble. Henry adds that just being noticed comforts hurting people, and that we should also ask why we ourselves are sad.

The men felt helpless, because in prison they had no one to explain their dreams. Joseph points them to God, since only God knows the future and so only he can give the meaning. Joseph takes no credit for himself. Still, he offers to help, because God had given him this gift.

The cupbearer dreams of a vine with three branches. It quickly buds, blossoms and ripens into grapes. He squeezes the grapes into Pharaoh's cup and hands it to him. The dream shows him back at his own job, in pictures he would easily understand.

Joseph explains that the three branches mean three days. Within that time Pharaoh will "lift up your head," a saying that means raising someone from disgrace and giving him back his post. Calvin says no one could guess that the branches meant days rather than years, so the meaning came from God's Spirit. Joseph spoke boldly, knowing that within three days everyone would see whether he was right.

Joseph asks the cupbearer to remember him and to tell Pharaoh his story. He simply says he was kidnapped and has done nothing wrong, without blaming his brothers, his master or his master's wife. Matthew Henry teaches that when we defend ourselves, we should try not to speak badly of others. Wanting to be free was not wrong, and Joseph took the way out that God seemed to offer.

Hearing the good news, the baker hopes for good news too and tells his dream. He carries three baskets on his head, and birds eat Pharaoh's baked goods out of the top one. Like the cupbearer's dream, it pictures his own job, but this time Pharaoh never gets the food. Calvin warns that many people want God's word only when they expect it to please them.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The word translated "white bread" is uncertain. Some read "wicker baskets," and evidence from the ancient city of Ebla suggests "pastries of white flour."

notes.meaning: Again, the three baskets mean three days. But this time "lift up your head" takes a terrible turn: Pharaoh will lift the baker's head off. He will be put to death, and his body will hang on a tree for the birds to eat. Joseph did not soften God's message, and Matthew Henry says that if a faithful message is unwelcome, it is not the messenger's fault.

On the third day, Pharaoh's birthday, he held a feast for all his officials. There he "lifted up the heads" of both men, which here means he brought their cases to trial. A king's birthday was a time to review officials and prisoners. Matthew Henry suggests we use our own birthdays to thank God for the gift of life.

Everything happened just as Joseph had said. The cupbearer got his job back, and the baker was hanged. This showed that Joseph was a true prophet, someone who speaks God's message, and that the meaning had come from God. Matthew Henry notes how quickly life can change, for better or for worse.

Sadly, the cupbearer forgot all about Joseph, who stayed in prison two more years. Matthew Henry calls this ingratitude and says, "We cannot expect too little from man, nor too much from God." Yet the writers see God's wise plan here: Joseph would be freed another way, so the glory would be God's. Matthew Henry compares this to Christ, who did not forget the thief who asked to be remembered, though Adam Clarke warned against forcing such comparisons.
